Issued at 308 PM EST Thu Nov 12 2026

This Afternoon through Friday Night...

Across the area this afternoon, temperatures are in the low-to-mid 
50s in most locations with breezy NW winds continuing in the wake of 
last night's cold front. Steepening low-level lapse rates combined 
with moisture in the 925-700 mb layer has allowed for the 
development of a broken stratocu field, with cloud cover filling in 
over the past few hours. A secondary mid-level vort max descending 
into the Ohio Valley this afternoon is supporting ascent in the low-
to-mid levels of the atmosphere, leading to the development of 
scattered rain showers. Sounding profiles from SDF show 100-200 J/kg 
of SBCAPE, and some of the showers have grown tall enough to produce 
graupel or small hail given freezing heights which are falling below 
1 km this afternoon.

Through early evening, scattered to numerous showers should continue 
to move from NW to SE across the area. The mid-level shortwave axis 
and a secondary cold front should push through the region this 
evening, bringing a reinforcing shot of cold advection. The shower 
activity should diminish with the loss of daytime heating and the 
passage of the trough axis this evening; however, another mid-level 
wave coming down from the Great Lakes tonight is expected to bring 
an area of deeper saturation, leading to more cloud cover and a 
return of shower chances by early Friday morning. Increasing low 
cloud cover overnight and persistent NW winds should keep 
temperatures from falling too much, with lows expected to range from 
the mid 30s to around 40 in most locations.

For the day on Friday, additional vort lobes are expected to 
pinwheel across the Midwest and Ohio Valley, bringing forcing for 
rising motion across the area. As referenced above, 12Z REFS 
guidance shows an area of deeper saturation (up to around 650 mb or -
15C) pivoting across the region during the late morning and early 
afternoon hours. This deeper saturation, combined with steep lapse 
rates, should allow for another round of scattered showers, 
especially east of I-65. Temperatures near the surface tomorrow will 
be around 10 degrees cooler than today, with many locations 
remaining in the low-to-mid 40s through much of the day. Model 
soundings show freezing levels falling to around 2-2.5k ft AGL 
tomorrow afternoon, with intermittent saturation into the DGZ. As a 
result, while the predominant p-type will be rain tomorrow, some 
brief transitions to or mixing with snow and/or graupel will be 
possible in the heaviest precipitation cores. No impacts are 
expected from wintry precipitation. Breezy NW winds will make things 
feel quite chilly tomorrow, with 10-15 mph winds expected through 
the day.

Friday evening, the broader area of low-to-mid level moisture will 
begin to eject off to the east, with some clearing likely across the 
area. We'll have to watch how persistent the Lake Michigan streamer 
band of moisture is, as that could bring additional clouds and 
flurries or sprinkles into Friday night. Temperatures should fall to 
around or just below freezing by sunrise Saturday.

This Weekend through the Middle of Next Week...

The broad mid- and upper-level trough over the eastern CONUS will 
start to pull out of the region on Saturday, with sfc high pressure 
descending toward the Ohio Valley from the NW. Upstream building of 
ridging aloft should strengthen the sfc high pressure, with a ~1035 
mb high expected over the region by Monday morning. This will allow 
a broad cP air mass to settle over the region this weekend, bringing 
below normal temperatures and dry air which will continue over the 
area into early next week.

Over the weekend, temperatures should be about 10 degrees below 
normal, with highs in the upper 40s and low 50s and lows in the mid-
20s to around 30. Daytime stratocu should re-develop on Saturday, 
and then potentially across the Bluegrass on Sunday; however, dry 
weather is expected.

For the first half of next week, omega blocking pattern will set up 
across the central CONUS, with sfc high pressure remaining just to 
the northeast of the region. The dry air mass in place will support 
large daily temperature swings from lows below freezing to highs in 
the 50s (60s possible by Wednesday). The omega block should start to 
break by next Wednesday-Thursday; however, any precipitation chances 
should remain to the NW of the area through the end of the current 
forecast period.
